etymology: American slang of the 1950s, of uncertain origin; the picture is of a man resting in cool shade while others labour in the sun, and the rhyme (made / shade) carried it. Often lengthened to "made in the shade with a glass of lemonade." Made here keeps the much older sense of "set up for life, assured of fortune" ("a made man"). Shade is Old English sceadu, shadow and shelter.
biblical_def: In 1956, if a fellow landed a steady job at the plant, a paid-off Chevrolet and a girl who said yes, his buddies said he had it made in the shade — nothing left to do but sit under a tree while the other fellows sweated in the sun. It is a happy phrase, and there is nothing wrong with thanking God for a good job and a quiet porch. But Scripture asks where the shade comes from. The Bible’s answer is that only one shade lasts: "The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand" (Psa 121:5). The man "that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty" (Psa 91:1). Our Lord told of a farmer who thought he had it made. He said to his soul, "take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry" (Luk 12:19) — and God answered, "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Luk 12:20). That is why Paul tells the comfortable not to "trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy" (1Ti 6:17). Grandchildren, the only man truly made in the shade is the one hidden in Christ. That shade does not move when the market moves or the plant closes, and it does not end at the grave.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1950s American) for being set for life, success assured — a picture of rest in cool shade that Scripture redirects to the only lasting shelter: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand (Psa 121:5).
webster_full: MADE IN THE SHADE, phrase (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; often "made in the shade with a glass of lemonade") Set for life; assured of success and ease. "New job, new car — he’s got it made in the shade."

Webster (1828) — SHADE, noun [Latin scutum , a shield.] 1. Literally, the interception, cutting of or interruption of the rays of light; hence, the obscurity which is caused by such interception. 2. Darkness; obscurity; as the shades of night. 3. An obscure place, properly in a grove or close wood, which precludes the sun’s rays; an hence, a secluded retreat. 4. A screen; something that intercepts light or heat. 5. Protection; shelter.
Decode for families: "made in the shade" means all set; the Psalm says who the real shade is.
scriptures: The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand.
Psa 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
corruption_summary: A cheerful phrase with little harm in it; the only danger is the one Jesus named — the rich farmer’s belief that ease once won is ease secured.
corruption_paragraphs: Most of the time made in the shade was simply a happy way to congratulate a friend, and a grandparent may say it with a clear conscience. Rejoicing with them that do rejoice is a Christian duty, and a man who has worked hard and been blessed may enjoy the shade God gives him.

The phrase does carry one quiet assumption: that comfort, once reached, is permanent. The rich farmer in Luke 12 made the same assumption and died that night. A family can keep the phrase and correct the assumption — whatever shade we enjoy is lent, and the only shelter that cannot be taken away is the LORD Himself, the shade upon our right hand.
roots_summary: Old English sceadu (shade, shelter) + made (set up, assured) → 1950s rhyme made in the shade → set for life.
roots_lines: Old English sceadu — shade, shadow, shelter from the sun
made — older English sense of set up, assured of fortune ("a made man")
1950s American slang: made in the shade — set for life, carried by the rhyme
Extended form: made in the shade with a glass of lemonade
Scripture: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand (Psa 121:5)
usage: "Dad paid off the house in ’57 and told Mother they were made in the shade."
The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand (Psa 121:5).
Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee (Luk 12:20).

etymology: American slang for a punch in the mouth, of uncertain origin and recorded by the mid-20th century; the joke pictures the fist as the "sandwich" served to the mouth. Knuckle is Middle English knokel, from a Germanic word for a joint or bone; sandwich takes its name from the 18th-century Earl of Sandwich. It was schoolyard and comic-strip talk for a generation — far more often threatened than delivered.
biblical_def: When a boy of 1950 said, "You want a knuckle sandwich?" he was offering to punch you in the mouth, and usually hoping he would not have to. Grandpa may have said it on a playground, and a few of us said it and meant it. It is worth stopping on, because Scripture has a good deal to say about the fist and the mouth. The Lord Jesus did not teach His people to serve knuckle sandwiches: "whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also" (Mat 5:39). That is not weakness; it is strength under rule. "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city" (Pro 16:32). The quickest way to end a fight is usually the mouth, not the fist: "A soft answer turneth away wrath" (Pro 15:1). And when we have truly been wronged, we are not left without justice: "avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19). Christ Himself was struck in the face by an officer of the high priest, and He answered with a word, not a blow. A Christian may defend the weak, and a father may protect his home; but the boy who learns to turn away wrath with a soft answer has learned something harder and better than throwing a punch.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (mid-century American) for a punch in the mouth — a schoolyard threat that Scripture answers with the stronger way of the soft word: A soft answer turneth away wrath (Pro 15:1).
webster_full: KNUCKLE SANDWICH, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s; schoolyard and comic-strip talk) A punch in the mouth, usually offered as a threat. "Keep it up and you’ll get a knuckle sandwich."
Webster (1828) — KNUCKLE, noun 1. The joint of a finger, particularly when protuberant by the closing of the fingers.
Decode for families: a threatened punch; Jesus taught the other cheek and the soft answer.
scriptures: Mat 5:39
But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.
He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
Jas 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
corruption_summary: A comic phrase that still dresses up a threat of violence as a joke, and Scripture calls the angry fist and the threatening mouth what they are.
corruption_paragraphs: Most knuckle sandwiches were never served; the phrase was bluster, half joke and half dare. Still, a threat is a threat, and it is spoken from the same heart that throws the punch. James says plainly that the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God, and the Lord counted the angry word in the same family as the blow (Mat 5:22).

There is an honest distinction to keep. Scripture does not forbid a man to protect the helpless, and the soldiers and policemen of that generation stood between their neighbours and harm. What it forbids is private revenge and the bully’s fist. Teach a boy the difference: strength is given to guard others, not to settle scores.
roots_summary: Middle English knokel (joint, knuckle bone) → knuckle (the fist) + sandwich → mid-century slang knuckle sandwich (a punch in the mouth).
roots_lines: Middle English knokel — a joint of the finger; Germanic root for bone
18th c.: sandwich — bread with a filling, named for the Earl of Sandwich
Mid-20th c. American slang: knuckle sandwich — a punch in the mouth, mostly threatened
Scripture: turn to him the other also (Mat 5:39)
usage: "Brother told the bully he’d get a knuckle sandwich — then Grandpa sat both boys down."
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger (Pro 15:1).
He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty (Pro 16:32).

etymology: American slang of the 1950s (also blow your lid, or simply flip), picturing a pot lid blown off by the steam beneath it. It meant either to lose one’s temper or to go wild with excitement — teenagers flipped their lids over a new record as readily as fathers flipped theirs over a dented fender. Lid is Old English hlid, a cover; flip, a quick toss, is recorded from the 16th century.
biblical_def: In 1955 flip your lid meant to lose control — a father who saw the dent in the Buick flipped his lid, and so did a teenager who heard a new rock and roll record for the first time. The picture is a pot on the stove: the heat rises, the pressure builds, and the lid flies off. Scripture uses a picture very like it: "He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls" (Pro 25:28). A man without a lid, like a city without walls, is open to every enemy. The Bible does not tell us never to feel heat. "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Eph 4:26). Anger at real wrong is not sin; anger that boils over is. So God gives the slow way: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath" (Jas 1:19), "For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God" (Jas 1:20). Grandchildren, the lid on the pot is not your own willpower. Temperance is called a fruit of the Spirit, because it grows in those who belong to Christ. The Lord Jesus was reviled and did not revile again; He kept His peace before His accusers, for us, and He gives that same Spirit to His people.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1950s American) for losing one’s temper or going wild — the pot lid blown off by steam, which Scripture pictures as a city that is broken down, and without walls (Pro 25:28).
webster_full: FLIP YOUR LID, phrase (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; also blow your lid, flip) To lose one’s temper; also, to go wild with excitement. "Dad’s going to flip his lid when he sees that fender."

Webster (1828) — LID, noun [Latin claudo, cludo; Gr.; Heb.] A cover; that which shuts the opening of a vessel or box; as the lid of a chest or trunk; also, the cover of the eye, the membrane which is drawn over the eyeball of an animal at pleasure, and which is intended for its protection; the eyelid.
Decode for families: to boil over; Scripture says a man without self-rule is a city without walls.
scriptures: He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
Eph 4:26
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
Jas 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
Jas 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
corruption_summary: When it means delight the phrase is harmless; when it means rage it names a real sin, the loss of rule over one’s own spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: Half the time a 1950s teenager flipped his lid with joy, and there is nothing to correct in that. The other half, it named a temper tantrum, and the slang made the tantrum sound like weather — something that simply happens to a man when the pressure gets high enough.

Scripture will not let us off that easily. The lid does not fly off by itself; the man who flips it has stopped ruling his spirit. The Christian answer is not to pretend we feel no heat but to bring it to God before the sun goes down, to confess the outburst plainly, and to ask the Spirit for the fruit of temperance.
roots_summary: Old English hlid (cover) → lid → 1950s flip your lid (the lid blown off by pressure) → to lose control.
roots_lines: Old English hlid — a cover, a lid
flip — to toss with a quick movement (16th c.)
1950s American slang: flip your lid, blow your lid — lose your temper or go wild
Scripture: he that ruleth his spirit (Pro 16:32)
usage: "When the Dodgers left Brooklyn, Uncle Ed flipped his lid for a week."
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath (Eph 4:26).
He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls (Pro 25:28).

etymology: Slang for a small child, of uncertain origin and recorded by the mid-20th century in American and Australian speech; it pictures a toddler at knee height — or lower — who nips at grown-ups’ heels like a puppy. Ankle is Old English ancleow; bite is Old English bitan. The word was usually affectionate, sometimes weary, and it belongs among the many fond names that the parents of the baby boom gave the little ones underfoot.
biblical_def: To a young father of 1955, the ankle biters were the little ones underfoot — crawling under the kitchen table, tugging at trouser legs, nipping at heels. The name was fond, and sometimes tired. Scripture takes the ankle biters far more seriously than the world does. "Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward" (Psa 127:3). They are not an interruption to life; they are one of God’s gifts in it. When the disciples treated the little ones as a nuisance, the Lord Jesus rebuked them: "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven" (Mat 19:14). Then "he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them" (Mar 10:16). He even set a child in the middle of grown men and said, "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven" (Mat 18:3). Grandchildren, you were ankle biters once, and to us you were treasures. A home full of little ones is loud and messy, and it is a home God has blessed. Pick them up, bless them, and bring them to Jesus.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (mid-century American) for a small child underfoot — a fond, weary nickname that Scripture lifts high: Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward (Psa 127:3).
webster_full: ANKLE BITER, n. (slang, mid-20th c.; popular with Silent Generation parents of the baby boom) A small child, especially a toddler underfoot. "Four ankle biters and one bathroom."
Webster (1828) — ANKLE, noun The joint which connects the foot with the leg.
Decode for families: a toddler; Jesus took them up in his arms and blessed them.
scriptures: Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.
But Jesus said, Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.
And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them.
Mat 18:3
And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: An affectionate nickname with little harm in it, though it can slide into treating children as pests rather than as the heritage of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing sinful about a playful name for a toddler, and most parents who used it said it with a smile. A tired mother may be forgiven for noticing that little ones bite ankles.

The quiet risk is in the attitude behind the joke. A joke repeated often enough shapes a heart, and a home that speaks of children mainly as trouble will begin to feel them as trouble. Scripture never treats children as pests. The disciples tried to send them away; Christ welcomed them. Keep the nickname warm, and keep the welcome warmer.
roots_summary: Old English ancleow (ankle) + bitan (bite) → mid-century slang ankle biter (a toddler underfoot).
roots_lines: Old English ancleow — the ankle joint
Old English bitan — to bite
Mid-20th c. slang: ankle biter — a small child at heel height
Scripture: of such is the kingdom of heaven (Mat 19:14)
usage: "Grandma raised five ankle biters on a mailman’s pay and never once complained."
Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD (Psa 127:3).
And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them (Mar 10:16).

etymology: American slang of the 1950s, from jazz and beat talk, where daddy (compare daddy-o) was a breezy address to any man and big daddy named the man in charge or the man everyone looked up to. Tennessee Williams’s play Cat on a Hot Tin Roof (1955) gave the name to its domineering patriarch, Big Daddy Pollitt, and the film of 1958 spread it widely. Dad itself is a child’s word for father, recorded from the 16th century.
biblical_def: In the slang of 1957, big daddy was the man in charge — the boss of the shop, the king of the dance floor, the fellow everyone deferred to. A famous play of the day made the name stick to a loud, domineering father who ruled his household by fear. Scripture asks what kind of man a man ought to be when others look up to him. The Lord Jesus warned against grasping for titles: "call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven" (Mat 23:9). He did not mean a boy may not call his own father Dad; He meant that no man may take the place of God. And He turned greatness upside down: "whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister" (Mar 10:43), and "whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all" (Mar 10:44). Those who lead the church are to rule as shepherds, not bosses, "being ensamples to the flock" (1Pe 5:3). The best news is that in Christ every believer has a true Father: "ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). Grandchildren, there is one Father above every big daddy on earth, and the best a grandfather can do is point you to Him and serve you as the Son of man came to serve.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1950s jazz and beat talk; spread by a 1955 play) for the man in charge or an admired older man — a title Christ redefines: whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister (Mar 10:43).
webster_full: BIG DADDY, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; from jazz and beat talk) The man in charge; an older man of authority or an admired figure. "Ask big daddy — he runs this shop."
Decode for families: the boss man; in Christ’s kingdom the greatest is the servant of all.
scriptures: Mat 23:9
And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister:
And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
Rom 8:15
For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.
corruption_summary: Mostly breezy and harmless, but the phrase can flatter the craving for rank that Christ rebuked, and its most famous bearer was a domineering father.
corruption_paragraphs: As a nickname for a respected older man, big daddy carried no harm, and plenty of grandfathers wore it with a grin. Honour to whom honour is due is a Bible principle, and a man who has earned respect may receive it.

The trouble lies in what the phrase admires. Big daddy is big because others serve him. Christ’s kingdom runs the other way: the Son of God washed feet. A father who wants to be great in his house should look to the Lord who came not to be ministered unto but to minister.
roots_summary: Child’s dad (father) → daddy → jazz and beat address (daddy-o) → 1950s big daddy (the man in charge).
roots_lines: dad — a child’s word for father, recorded from the 16th c.
1940s–50s jazz and beat talk: daddy, daddy-o — breezy address to a man
1955: Big Daddy Pollitt in Tennessee Williams’s Cat on a Hot Tin Roof
1950s slang: big daddy — the boss, the admired older man
Scripture: one is your Father, which is in heaven (Mat 23:9)
usage: "The foreman was big daddy on the line, but he still punched the clock like everybody else."
And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven (Mat 23:9).
And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all (Mar 10:44).

etymology: American rhyming slang for a bald man, of uncertain origin and recorded by the mid-20th century; the gleam of a bald head is compared to the chrome trim of the automobiles of the day. Chrome is short for chromium, named from Greek chroma, colour; dome, from Latin domus by way of Italian and French, had long been slang for the head.
biblical_def: In the age of tail fins and chrome bumpers, a bald man was a chrome dome — his head shone like the trim on a new Cadillac. It was usually friendly ribbing between men, and many a grandfather laughed at it about himself. But Scripture has a story every child should hear before using it. When the prophet Elisha walked to Bethel, "there came forth little children out of the city, and mocked him, and said unto him, Go up, thou bald head" (2Ki 2:23). They were not teasing a man for his hair; they were mocking the LORD’s prophet, and God judged it. Mockery of a person’s body is never a small thing. The law of Moses said plainly, "the man whose hair is fallen off his head, he is bald; yet is he clean" (Lev 13:40) — baldness is no shame. And God counts what is left: "even the very hairs of your head are all numbered" (Luk 12:7). A bare crown is a mark of years, and years walked with God are honourable: "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" (Pro 16:31). Grandchildren, when Grandpa’s head shines, let it remind you that the Lord numbered every hair he lost, and that a long life lived for Christ is a crown, not a joke.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (mid-century American) for a bald man, his head shining like chrome trim — friendly ribbing that Scripture tempers: The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31).
webster_full: CHROME DOME, n. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; the age of chrome bumpers) A bald man; a shining bald head. "Hey, chrome dome, you’re blinding the umpire."
Decode for families: a bald fellow; Scripture says he is clean, and every lost hair was numbered.
scriptures: And he went up from thence unto Bethel: and as he was going up by the way, there came forth little children out of the city, and mocked him, and said unto him, Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head.
And the man whose hair is fallen off his head, he is bald; yet is he clean.
Luk 12:7
But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
corruption_summary: Often good-natured ribbing among friends, but it is mockery of a man’s body, and Scripture treats mockery as more serious than we do.
corruption_paragraphs: Between old friends who both know the joke, chrome dome can be a kind of affection, and a man who laughs at his own bald head shows a healthy humility.

The same words from a child to a stranger, or from a crowd to one boy, are something else. Mocking a body God made is a small contempt for the Maker. The children at Bethel learned that the hard way. Teach the young to keep the joke for those who invite it, and to honour the old, whatever their hair is doing.
roots_summary: Greek chroma (colour) → chromium, chrome (car trim) + dome (head) → mid-century rhyming slang chrome dome (a bald man).
roots_lines: Greek chroma — colour; whence chromium, the shining plating metal
Latin domus → dome — a rounded roof; slang for the head
Mid-20th c.: chrome dome — a bald man, from the gleaming car trim of the era
Scripture: he is bald; yet is he clean (Lev 13:40)
usage: "Grandpa called himself chrome dome before anybody else could."
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31).
But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered (Luk 12:7).

etymology: Cootie was First World War soldiers’ slang for the body louse, recorded from about 1917 and probably from Malay kutu, a biting insect. In the trenches it was a real misery. By the 1940s and 1950s American schoolchildren had turned it into a playground game — imaginary germs passed by touch, usually between boys and girls — and a board game called Cootie (1949) kept the word in the toy closet.
biblical_def: When Grandpa was in third grade, if a girl touched his sleeve at recess he hollered that he had cooties, and every boy ran from him until somebody gave him a "cootie shot." It was a game, and most of us outgrew it by junior high. The word itself came home from the trenches of the First World War, where real lice tormented real soldiers. Scripture takes up both halves of the game. First, boys and girls are not each other’s contamination. "God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27). Paul tells young Timothy to treat "the younger as sisters, with all purity" (1Ti 5:2) — neither running from them nor chasing them. Second, the game is about who is clean and who is not, and that is where the gospel shines. In Israel a leper really was unclean, and everyone kept away. But when a leper came to Jesus, He did the unthinkable: "Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean" (Mat 8:3). The Lord does not run from the unclean; He touches them and makes them clean. So Paul says, "receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God" (Rom 15:7). Grandchildren, never make a game of treating another child as untouchable. Christ touched us.
webster_summary: Playground slang (1940s–50s; from the First World War word for lice) for imaginary germs of the opposite sex — a game of who is unclean that the gospel answers: Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him (Mat 8:3).
webster_full: COOTIES, n. pl. (Silent Generation playground slang, 1940s–50s; from First World War cootie, a louse) Imaginary germs passed by touch, especially between boys and girls. "Eww, she touched you — you’ve got cooties!"
Decode for families: pretend germs; Christ touched the truly unclean and made them clean.
scriptures: Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.
Mat 8:3
And Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean. And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.
Rom 15:7
Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God.
corruption_summary: Mostly innocent play, though the game can harden into shunning one child as untouchable, which is the opposite of what Christ did.
corruption_paragraphs: Little boys and girls running from each other at recess is about as innocent as childhood gets, and grandparents can laugh at the memory. The game even kept a modest distance between the sexes at an age when that distance is fitting.

The danger comes when cooties stop being shared by everyone and get pinned on one child — the poor one, the odd one, the one with the wrong clothes. Then the game becomes shunning, and the child learns he is unclean. Christian families should watch for that and stop it, because the Lord’s way with the outcast is to reach out and touch.
roots_summary: Malay kutu (biting insect, probable) → First World War cootie (a louse) → 1940s–50s playground cooties (imaginary germs).
roots_lines: Malay kutu — a biting insect (probable source)
c. 1917: cootie — soldiers’ word for the body louse in the trenches
1949: the board game Cootie
1940s–50s playground: cooties — pretend germs; the cootie shot as cure
Scripture: I will; be thou clean (Mat 8:3)
usage: "Sally sat next to Bobby in the lunchroom and he swore he caught cooties."
Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God (Rom 15:7).
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity (1Ti 5:2).

etymology: American slang for "sit down," recorded by the mid-20th century. Cop is old cant for to take or catch (whence cop, the policeman who catches), and squat, from Old French esquatir (to press down), is to crouch; so to cop a squat is to take a seat. It was a breezy invitation among servicemen, students and soda-fountain regulars.
biblical_def: "Cop a squat" was how a friend said "sit down" in 1952 — at the soda fountain, in the barracks, around the kitchen table. It is a friendly phrase, an invitation to stay a while. Scripture is full of sitting, and much of it is holy. The peace God promised His people was a picture of sitting: "they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid" (Mic 4:4). Mary of Bethany chose the best seat in the house — at the Lord’s feet, where she "heard his word" (Luk 10:39). Where we sit also shows our hearts. The Lord told guests at a feast to "go and sit down in the lowest room" (Luk 14:10) rather than grab the best chair. And the greatest sitting of all is Christ’s. Having finished His work on the cross, He sat down at the right hand of the Father, as David foretold: "Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool" (Psa 110:1). Because He sits, His people may rest: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). Grandchildren, when Grandpa tells you to cop a squat, he is offering you a place at his table. The Lord offers a better one, and it is never full.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (mid-century American) for "sit down" — a friendly invitation that recalls the rest God promised: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree (Mic 4:4).
webster_full: COP A SQUAT, phrase (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; barracks, campus and soda-fountain talk) Sit down; take a seat. "Cop a squat and tell me how the game went."
Webster (1828) — SQUAT, verb intransitive 1. To sit down upon the hams or heels; as a human being. 2. To sit close to the ground; to cower; as an animal.
Decode for families: have a seat; the Lord says take the lowest room, and come to Him for rest.
scriptures: Mic 4:4
But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid: for the mouth of the LORD of hosts hath spoken it.
And she had a sister called Mary, which also sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word.

But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee.
A Psalm of David. The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
corruption_summary: A harmless and friendly phrase; the only thing to watch is the old habit of grabbing the best seat, which Jesus corrected.
corruption_paragraphs: There is nothing to correct in cop a squat. It is hospitality in slang — pull up a chair, you are welcome here — and hospitality is a Christian virtue.

The only lesson hiding in it is about where we sit. Jesus watched guests pick the chief seats and told them to take the lowest place instead. A child who learns to offer the good chair to Grandma has learned the parable.
roots_summary: Old cant cop (to take, catch) + Old French esquatir → squat (crouch) → mid-century cop a squat (take a seat).
roots_lines: 18th c. cant: cop — to take, to catch
Old French esquatir — to press down, flatten → English squat
Mid-20th c. American slang: cop a squat — sit down
Scripture: go and sit down in the lowest room (Luk 14:10)
usage: "Cop a squat, son — your grandmother’s bringing the pie."
But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree (Mic 4:4).
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Mat 11:28).

etymology: American slang for a state of comfort and plenty ("we’re in fat city"), of uncertain origin and date; it is recorded in print from the 1960s. Leonard Gardner’s novel Fat City (1969) used the phrase with bitter irony for the good life his down-and-out boxers never reach. Fat has meant rich and plentiful since Old English, as in the King James "the fat of the land."
biblical_def: To be in fat city was to have it good — the raise came through, the car was paid for, the icebox was full. It is a thankful-sounding phrase, and Scripture does not despise plenty. God gave Israel a good land and told them what to do when they reached fat city: "When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee" (Deu 8:10). But the next breath is a warning: "Beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God" (Deu 8:11). Plenty is the place where people most easily forget God. The wise man of Proverbs prayed for neither too little nor too much, "Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD?" (Pro 30:9). Paul learned the secret of both lean years and fat ones: "I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound" (Php 4:12). And the Lord Jesus put a fence around every fat city: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness" (Luk 12:15). Grandchildren, our generation lived through the Depression and then came into more plenty than our parents dreamed of. The lesson we learned, and sometimes forgot, is that fat city is a good place to give thanks and a dangerous place to live without God. The true riches are in Christ, who became poor that we through His poverty might be rich.
webster_summary: Mid-century American slang for a state of comfort and plenty — a good place to give thanks and a dangerous place to forget, for God said, Beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God (Deu 8:11).
webster_full: FAT CITY, n. (American slang, mid-20th c.; recorded in print from the 1960s) A state of comfort, plenty and ease. "With the overtime coming in, we’re in fat city."
Decode for families: living well; plenty is a call to bless the LORD, not to forget Him.
scriptures: Deu 8:10
When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God for the good land which he hath given thee.
Deu 8:11
Beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God, in not keeping his commandments, and his judgments, and his statutes, which I command thee this day:
Pro 30:9
Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.
Php 4:12
I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
corruption_summary: A cheerful phrase for being well off; the only danger is the one Moses named — that full bellies forget God.
corruption_paragraphs: Thanking God for a good season is right, and a family that has come into plenty may say so without guilt. Many of the grandparents who used this phrase had known real hunger in the 1930s; for them, fat city was a mercy, and they knew it.

The phrase can also become a destination, as if the point of life were to arrive in fat city and stay. Scripture never treats wealth as the goal. It is a trust to be used, shared and given back. The novel that borrowed the name used it as irony, and the irony is fitting: fat city is never quite where people think it is.
roots_summary: Old English fat (plump, rich) → "the fat of the land" → mid-century slang fat city (comfort and plenty).
roots_lines: Old English fat — plump; rich, plentiful
KJV idiom: ye shall eat the fat of the land (Gen 45:18)
Mid-20th c. American slang: fat city — easy street, plenty
1969: Leonard Gardner’s novel Fat City, using the phrase with irony
usage: "After the war Dad got on at the plant, and for a while we were in fat city."
When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God (Deu 8:10).
I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound (Php 4:12).

etymology: From flicker, the unsteady light of early motion pictures; the flicks for "the movies" is recorded from the 1920s, first in British use, and Americans of the 1940s and 1950s used a flick for a single film. Flick itself, a light quick stroke, is centuries older and imitative in origin.
biblical_def: For a teenager in 1950, Saturday meant a flick — a quarter for the double feature, a newsreel, a cartoon and a box of popcorn. The word came from the flicker of the early projectors. Grandparents remember when most films were clean enough to take a child to, and when that began to change. Scripture does not mention the movies, but it speaks plainly about what we set before our eyes. David resolved, "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3), and prayed, "Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity; and quicken thou me in thy way" (Psa 119:37). The Lord Jesus taught that the eye is a lamp: "if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Mat 6:22). What comes in through a screen goes somewhere. Paul gives a family the test for every flick: "whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely… think on these things" (Php 4:8). And because our hours are short, we are to be found "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16). Grandchildren, a good story well told is a gift, and there is no sin in an evening at the pictures with your family. Choose the flick the way you would choose a guest for the house, because that is what it is.
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1940s–50s, from the flicker of early projectors) for a movie — a pleasure Scripture governs by one plain rule: I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psa 101:3).
webster_full: FLICK, n. (slang, from 1920s the flicks; an everyday Silent Generation word 1940s–50s) A motion picture, a movie. "Want to catch a flick at the Bijou Saturday?"
Decode for families: a movie; choose it the way you would choose a guest for the house.
scriptures: I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.
Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity; and quicken thou me in thy way.
Mat 6:22
The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.
Php 4:8

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Eph 5:16
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
corruption_summary: A neutral word for a movie; the concern lies not in the word but in what a generation learned to set before its eyes.
corruption_paragraphs: Flick itself is innocent, and so is a good film. Stories, music and pictures are gifts of a creative God, and families have long enjoyed them together.

What changed over the grandparents’ lifetime was the content, and the habit of watching whatever was playing. The eye is a door to the heart. A Christian home needs no long list of forbidden titles so much as a settled rule — true, honest, just, pure, lovely — and the courage to walk out of the theatre when a film breaks it.
roots_summary: flick (a light, quick stroke) → flicker (unsteady light) → 1920s the flicks (the movies) → 1940s–50s a flick (a film).
roots_lines: Imitative flick — a quick light blow, 15th c.
flicker — to waver, flutter; the shaky light of early film
1920s: the flicks — the movies (British first, then American)
1940s–50s: a flick — one film; the Saturday double feature
Scripture: Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity (Psa 119:37)
usage: "We saw a flick at the Rialto, then split a malt at the drugstore."
I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes (Psa 101:3).
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil (Eph 5:16).

etymology: American slang for angry or annoyed, of uncertain origin and heard in mid-century teen talk; the picture is the cold stare and frozen tone of someone displeased (compare frosty, icy, the cold shoulder, and "it frosts me"). The ordinary sense — covered with frost, or iced like a cake — is much older; frost is Old English.
biblical_def: In 1957, if your sister was frosted, she was steaming mad but not saying much — arms crossed, chin up, the cold shoulder at the supper table. It is a different picture from the hot temper of flip your lid: this is anger gone cold. Scripture speaks to both. God permits anger at wrong, but not anger kept on ice: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath" (Eph 4:26). Cold anger is exactly the kind that outlasts a sunset. Paul names its frozen relatives and tells us to put them away: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice" (Eph 4:31). The remedy is warm: "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another" (Eph 4:32), because God in Christ has forgiven us. Frost has its place in God’s world — "By the breath of God frost is given" (Job 37:10) — but it belongs on the window pane, not in the heart. Grandchildren, when you feel yourself freezing toward a brother, do what the Lord said and go to him before the day is out. A soft word thaws more ice than a long silence: "A soft answer turneth away wrath" (Pro 15:1).
webster_summary: Silent Generation slang (1950s American teen talk) for angry, especially coldly angry — the frozen silence that Scripture tells us to thaw before nightfall: let not the sun go down upon your wrath (Eph 4:26).
webster_full: FROSTED, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; teen talk) Angry, annoyed, especially in a cold and silent way. "Don’t talk to Linda — she’s frosted about the dance."

Webster (1828) — FROST, noun 1. A fluid congealed by cold into ice or crystals; as hoar-frost, which is dew or vapor congealed. 2. The act of freezing; congelation of fluids. FROST, verb transitive 1. In cookery, to cover or sprinkle with a composition of sugar, resembling hoar-frost; as, to frost cake.
Decode for families: mad and freezing you out; Scripture says thaw it before sundown.
scriptures: Eph 4:26
Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath:
Eph 4:31
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
Eph 4:32
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
By the breath of God frost is given: and the breadth of the waters is straitened.
Pro 15:1
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
corruption_summary: The word names a real sin — anger nursed in cold silence — though in slang it was often used lightly for mere annoyance.
corruption_paragraphs: Plenty of times frosted meant only peeved, and a peeve that passes by evening is no great matter. The slang is not wicked; it is honest about a feeling.

But the cold anger it describes is one of the most destructive things in a family. Hot tempers flare and fade; frozen ones last for years, between brothers, between husbands and wives, between churches. Scripture treats the unresolved grudge as giving place to the devil (Eph 4:27). A Christian home can teach children to name it — I am frosted — and then to bring it to God and to the one they are angry with.
roots_summary: Old English forst, frost (frozen dew) → frosted (frost-covered, iced) → 1950s slang frosted (coldly angry).
roots_lines: Old English forst, frost — freezing cold; frozen dew
frosted — covered with frost; iced, as a cake
Figurative: frosty, icy, the cold shoulder — coolness of manner
1950s American teen slang: frosted — angry, peeved
Scripture: By the breath of God frost is given (Job 37:10)
usage: "Mother was frosted all afternoon after Dad forgot their anniversary."
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice (Eph 4:31).
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another (Eph 4:32).

etymology: American underworld slang for the police, recorded from 1929 and of unknown origin; the guesses offered for it are unproven. It spread in the 1950s through jazz and hipster talk and became a staple of 1960s crime films and television. The older fuzz — light fibres, down — is a separate word, and it is that sense Webster recorded in 1828.
biblical_def: When a hipster of 1958 warned, "Cool it — here comes the fuzz," he meant the police, and he did not mean it kindly. The word came out of the underworld, where the officer was the enemy. Many of the grandparents who heard it had sons and brothers who walked a beat, and they knew better. Scripture does not let a Christian speak of lawful authority with a sneer. "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God" (Rom 13:1). The policeman on the corner is, in Paul’s words, "the minister of God to thee for good" (Rom 13:4). That does not make every officer righteous; magistrates answer to God for how they bear the sword. But it does settle how we speak: "Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king" (1Pe 2:17). Believers are to be ready "to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work" (Tit 3:1). Grandchildren, the only people who need to fear the police are those doing evil. The Lord Jesus, who will one day judge every judge, submitted to unjust rulers for our sake, and He calls us to pray for those in authority rather than mock them.
webster_summary: American underworld slang (recorded 1929; spread by 1950s hipsters) for the police — a sneer Scripture corrects, since the lawful officer is the minister of God to thee for good (Rom 13:4).
webster_full: FUZZ, n. (American slang, from 1929 underworld use; hipster talk in the 1950s, everywhere by the 1960s) The police. "Somebody called the fuzz on the drag racers."
Webster (1828) — FUZZ, noun Fine, light particles; loose, volatile matter.
Decode for families: the police, said with a sneer; Scripture says honour the one who keeps the peace.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
Tit 3:1
Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work,
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change:
corruption_summary: A word born in contempt for lawful authority, which Scripture forbids even while it permits honest grief over wrongdoers in uniform.
corruption_paragraphs: Fuzz was never a neutral word. It came from men who lived outside the law, and it carried their scorn into the mouths of teenagers who only wanted to sound tough. Speaking evil of dignities is something Scripture names and rebukes (Jud 1:8).

Honesty requires one more word. Officers sin like other men, and a Christian may grieve over abuse of power and seek justice through lawful means. But a family can do that without adopting the vocabulary of the underworld. Call them police officers, pray for them by name, and teach the children that the man in blue who runs toward danger is serving his neighbours.
roots_summary: Origin unknown → 1929 American underworld fuzz (the police) → 1950s hipster talk → 1960s everyday slang.
roots_lines: fuzz — light fibres, down; a separate, older word
1929: fuzz — the police, in American criminal slang; origin unknown
1950s jazz and hipster talk: the fuzz
Scripture: Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king (1Pe 2:17)
usage: "Grandpa walked a beat for thirty years and never once called himself the fuzz."
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers (Rom 13:1).
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king (Pro 24:21).
